analysis.one_liner: Creates the first federal right to keep your medical records confidential, with criminal penalties for wrongful disclosure.
analysis.headline: The Senate health committee held hearings on the bill but never voted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 without any health privacy law passing.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created the first nationwide rules for who can see and share your medical records. It gave people the right to see, copy, and correct their own health information, required organizations to post notices of their confidentiality practices and keep records of disclosures, and added criminal penalties for misusing health data. But it also let a single authorization signed at health-plan enrollment cover most uses, gave life insurers enforcement only through state insurance commissioners, offered patients no right to sue in court, and would have overridden state privacy laws. The Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients would gain federal rights to inspect, copy, and request corrections to their medical records, plus notices explaining who can see their information and criminal penalties of up to $250,000 and 10 years for disclosures made for profit or malicious harm. Health plans, insurers, and providers would also gain one uniform federal standard replacing a patchwork of state rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, and insurers wanting one national standard

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals the right to inspect and copy their own protected health information held by providers, plans, employers, life insurers, schools, and universities, with written explanations if access is denied [S3].
Requires written notice of each organization's confidentiality practices and administrative, technical, and physical safeguards for health data, plus a 7-year record of disclosures [S3].

Imposes criminal penalties for wrongful disclosure: up to $50,000 and one year in prison, up to $100,000 and five years under false pretenses, and up to $250,000 and ten years when done for monetary gain or malicious harm [S3].
Restricts for the first time how employers may handle employee health information, barring release to staff who make hiring, promotion, and work-assignment decisions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Doctors, hospitals, insurers, employers, and schools would bear the cost of building safeguards, posting notices, tracking disclosures, and obtaining authorizations. Patients whose records were misused would have no right to sue — the bill immunizes permitted disclosures from common-law liability and leaves punishment to the Health and Human Services Department and state regulators.
analysis.who_pays_short: Providers, insurers, employers bearing compliance costs

drawbacks.text: There is no private right of action: the bill shields permissible disclosures from common-law liability, so an individual harmed by misuse of records could not sue, relying instead on penalties imposed by the Secretary of Health and Human Services [S3].
The bill would preempt state laws covering the same subject matter, replacing stronger state protections in areas such as mental health and other sensitive records with the federal floor [S3].

A single authorization obtained at the time of enrollment in an employer or health plan covers use and disclosure for treatment, payment, and health care operations — which includes underwriting and utilization review — meaning consent is given once, up front, for a broad range of uses [S3].
Enforcement against life insurers is given exclusively to the insurance commissioner of the insurer's home state under state insurance procedures, the industry's usual regulator [S3].

Banks, credit unions, and payment-card processors are exempted from the Act for payment transactions and left to banking regulators instead, keeping health information flowing through payment systems with weaker privacy enforcement [S3].
A health plan may terminate an enrollee's coverage if revoking the authorization leaves the plan unable to provide care or conduct operations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real, new protections for a kind of record that previously had almost no federal privacy law at all, and its criminal penalties were serious. But its enforcement design left patients dependent on regulators and state insurance commissioners rather than courts, its single enrollment-time authorization was broad, and its preemption clause would have replaced some stronger state protections. Whether that trade was worth it was the central argument of the 1999 privacy debate, and the Senate never resolved it because the bill never came to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee, which held hearings but never voted to send it to the floor, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 — Congress never passed a health privacy law, and privacy rules were instead issued by the Health and Human Services Department under the timetable set by the 1996 portability law.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Bennett introduced the bill on April 27, 1999, joined by Sens. Mack, Murkowski, and Santorum as original cosponsors [S3].
The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which held hearings printed as S.Hrg. 106-64 [S5].
The committee never voted the bill out and the Senate never debated it; the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1].
The bill would have created rights to inspect, copy, and amend health records, mandated confidentiality safeguards, restricted disclosures, and set criminal and civil penalties [S2].
It would have preempted state laws on the same subject and given state insurance commissioners exclusive enforcement authority over life insurers [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, health insurers, life insurers, banks, and employers avoided new criminal penalties and continued under the existing mix of state rules and later federal regulations, without facing patient lawsuits. Patients went without any federal statutory medical privacy rights from Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill gives plans a single uniform federal standard, lets one enrollment-time authorization cover treatment, payment, and operations including underwriting, preempts stricter state rules, and blocks patient lawsuits. Ordinary people would have gained some privacy rights, but at the cost of weaker, regulator-only enforcement.

Enforcement against life insurers would rest exclusively with the insurance commissioner of the insurer's home state under state insurance procedures, keeping the industry with its usual regulator rather than facing federal prosecutors or lawsuits.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and payment processors
industries.note: Entities handling health care payments by card or electronic means are exempted from the Act's penalties and left to banking and securities regulators, keeping medical details flowing through payment systems under lighter privacy rules.

Providers take on real duties — safeguards, notices, disclosure accounting, and authorizations — but gain one national standard instead of 50 state regimes and protection from common-law lawsuits for permitted disclosures.

The bill for the first time walls off employee health information from staff who make hiring and promotion decisions, but employers offering health plans still obtain broad enrollment-time authorizations and escape state law preemption risk.
Researchers can obtain records through institutional review board approval or internal data-use agreements, and are shielded from being compelled to disclose research data in court proceedings.
